steps.npc: Well, friend, I'm Arls Lutwidge of the Moonlight Broadsword! Renowned all over Gielinor!

steps.player: Can't say I've heard of you before.

steps.npc: You haven't... heard of... That's madness!
Surely you've heard of my feats, but perhaps not the name?
And yourself?

steps.player: An adventurer mostly, but I've slain some dragons and I've conquered some nightmares.

steps.npc: Very good, young one! Very good indeed!

steps.player: So... where's this famous sword of yours?

steps.npc: Gone. I gave it to a fledgling when I retired and the damned fool went and died fighting some great monster in a far off land.
Say... if you find it, could you bring it to me? I won't pay you, as holding such a magnificent weapon should be payment enough.

steps.player: I think you need to work on your bartering skills.

steps.npc: Perhaps.

options.text: What grand feats are you known for?

steps.player: What grand feats are you known for?

steps.npc: I peaked rather early and most know me for my first act of heroism when I defeated the Moonfly. It may sound cute, but it killed many of the smallfolk and their livestock, for it was a vile creature.
It was I that discovered the creature. I pulled it from the Lum during a fishing trip of mine.
As young and foolish as I was, I dropped it down a dried up well and went for help. However, upon my return, the creature was gone.
Many years passed until suddenly there were sightings of a winged demon around the River Lum. Some claimed it was an overly large heron and that it was nothing to be worried about.
As time went on, folk started to go missing and I knew I had to return home and face this demon.
I had wars to fight, glory to be won and all that rubbish. Upon my return I spoke to an old crone who lived in the swamps and she gave me some advice.
She told me to spike my armour and described how to lure the creature toward me.

steps.player: And you defeated it? The Moonfly?

steps.npc: Some bard wrote a poem of the events. The telling of the battle is a little embellished and rife with errors. The poem can be found in this library somewhere, providing it has been returned.
And did I defeat the creature? I wouldn't be here if I hadn't!

steps.player: I'll be sure to keep an eye out.

steps.npc: Please do! And come to me if you have any burning questions about it.
I've grown old, friend. Heroes need to know when to throw in the towel, so they say. I've always enjoyed a good book, so it seemed fitting to stay here as librarian for the guild.

steps.player: Hmm... the books are very interesting. I thought there would be more though...

steps.npc: Well, that's why I'm here! So many of you adventurers help yourself to any old book and never return the damn things!
If I could have it my way, you wouldn't be allowed to wander off with them, but I'm not the guildmaster, as Alec likes to remind me.

steps.player: Certainly sounds like you have a problem.

steps.npc: Well fear not. I'm working on it!
I'll see you around.

using-lutwidge-and-the-moonfly-on-lutwid.npc: Yes! Fantastic! Did you enjoy it?

using-lutwidge-and-the-moonfly-on-lutwid.player: Yeah it was alright. Some of these words are a bit odd though. Did you really cover your sword in sheep blood?

using-lutwidge-and-the-moonfly-on-lutwid.npc: Ah, a slight misunderstanding... I soaked it in sap from a yew tree, but I guess blood is a bit more dramatic.
The crone, long dead now, I suppose... She claimed to be from the same world as the creature and knew of the ritual to summon it.

using-lutwidge-and-the-moonfly-on-lutwid.player: The poem does mention sheep though, at the end?

using-lutwidge-and-the-moonfly-on-lutwid.npc: Perhaps some locals claimed to have lost some sheep, but my guess is that the bard was searching for a rhyme. Either way, I doubt it's a detail worth fretting over.
